paras: The attempted lynching of J. H. Floyd took place in Arizona Territory in May 1881, when armed men from Florence pursued Sheriff J. P. Gabriel and his prisoner to Casa Grande and demanded Floyd at gunpoint. Floyd had been arrested for shooting dead an elderly Florence resident, Charles Bernard, known as "American Charley." The sheriff held off the party until a train arrived and lodged Floyd in the Tucson jail; Floyd was later convicted of manslaughter, a verdict Arizona papers denounced so sharply that one regretted the lynching had failed.

According to a Tucson dispatch dated May 17, Floyd shot and instantly killed Bernard at Florence on the night of Sunday, May 15, 1881, a date later accounts of the trial repeated. In its October account, the Citizen wrote that Bernard was seated in the door of his room when Floyd, "crazed with liquor," turned in the street and shot him. The killing, the Citizen said, roused "the spirit of summary vengeance" in Florence, and its people "immediately organized with the intention of lynching the murderer."

Anticipating the move, Sheriff Gabriel took Floyd out of Florence in broad daylight toward Casa Grande, on the way to Tucson for safekeeping. A party from Florence learned of the departure, followed, took the sheriff by surprise, and with "leveled guns at his breast" demanded the prisoner. The Citizen put the party at eight or ten men; Gabriel refused them and secured other help, and the men withdrew to consult.

Gabriel kept watch through the night until the train reached Casa Grande, and the Tucson dispatch said a posse helped him put Floyd aboard. Floyd reached Tucson the next morning and was placed in the county jail. A telegram from Florence, also dated May 17, summed up the episode: a mob had tried to take Floyd from the sheriff "but were unsuccessful." No one was reported hurt, and no report of arrests of the men who confronted the sheriff appears in the coverage.

When the district court met at Florence in October under Judge Stilwell, Floyd was among the prisoners brought from jail to answer for the killing. His defense, as the Florence Arizona Weekly Enterprise reported it, was that Bernard had asked him for two dollars and struck him with a club, so that he fired in self-defense. After about twenty minutes the jury returned a verdict of manslaughter, and Floyd was sentenced to five years.

The Prescott Weekly Arizona Miner then reported that the murderer of American Charley had "escaped." The Enterprise replied that Andrew Hall had taken Floyd to Yuma and lodged him in the Territorial prison, and that only the light sentence could be called an "escape."

The Tucson dispatch ran in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Los Angeles Herald on May 18 and in the Eureka Daily Sentinel and Unionville Silver State in Nevada on May 19 and 20. It called the killing "cold-blooded" and "without any justification," and the Eureka paper headed it "Murder and Attempted Lynching."

The Arizona Citizen's own story, headlined "Plucky Pete," centered on the sheriff, whom it called "the brave officer," and the Los Angeles Herald reprinted it on May 19. Its comment was divided: the retribution the "indignant citizens" intended would have been "merited justice," yet good citizens should aid an officer doing his duty.

The verdict hardened that tone. Under the heading "A Travesty of Justice," the Citizen wrote that it was "almost a matter of regret" that the lynching had not been carried out. The Enterprise, published at Florence, called Floyd a "hell-deserving dastard" who deserved "having his neck jerked out of joint" rather than five years at Yuma. None of the reports identified Floyd, Bernard or the men from Florence by race.

Two versions of the shooting appeared: the Citizen's, in which Floyd shot a man sitting quietly in his doorway, and Floyd's own, presented at trial, in which Bernard attacked him with a club. The Enterprise said Floyd's statement was unsupported by any witness and that proof of a deliberate murder existed but was not introduced at the trial. A Sacramento news digest placed the conviction at Prescott, while the Pinal County papers reported the trial at Florence.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of J. H. Floyd
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: An organized party of armed men from Florence pursued the sheriff and demanded his prisoner at gunpoint with the stated intention of lynching him, but failed (A2, A7, A9); this is an attempted lynching, and no report gives the race of anyone involved.

Eight or ten men acting without authority tried to seize Floyd to punish him for a killing (A9), a lynching attempt under the pretext of justice, but no one was killed by the mob: Floyd was delivered to the Tucson jail and later sentenced to prison (A9, A11, A16).
The Tucson wire dispatch (A2), a separate Florence telegram (A7) and the Tucson Citizen's local account (A9) independently report the mob's failed attempt to take Floyd from the sheriff.

framing.detail: The Tucson dispatch ran in California and Nevada papers, headed 'Murder and Attempted Lynching' in Eureka, and called the killing 'cold-blooded'.
The Tucson Citizen's 'Plucky Pete' praised 'the brave officer' for resisting the mob while saying the intended retribution would have been 'merited justice'.

After the manslaughter verdict the Citizen's 'A Travesty of Justice' said it was 'almost a matter of regret' the lynching was not carried out, and the Florence Enterprise said Floyd deserved 'having his neck jerked out of joint'.
